overview: A powerful nor'easter hit the East Coast on Thanksgiving, knocking out power to hundreds of thousands, delaying thousands of flights and pushing Macy's centennial parade to Saturday. In Washington, President Trump called recent GDP figures "fake" and demanded an investigation of the Commerce Department, while a federal judge blocked the FCC's early review of ABC's station licenses. Abroad, a drone attack that officials attributed to Iran killed two Italian contractors in Kuwait, though Iran denied involvement, and New Zealand's ruling coalition fell short of a majority in final election results. Markets are still digesting Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia's chief executive, which has whipsawed tech stocks around the world.

stories.headline: Thanksgiving storm cuts power to hundreds of thousands and postpones Macy's parade
stories.summary: A powerful storm brought heavy rain, high winds and coastal flooding to the East Coast on Thanksgiving, knocking out power to hundreds of thousands of customers and disrupting holiday travel. Macy's postponed its 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York to Saturday, the first weather postponement in its history. Conditions were expected to improve gradually on Friday, though Pennsylvania and nearby states were still badly affected.
stories.why_it_matters: Anyone traveling home after the holiday on the East Coast may still face delays and outages, and people in the hardest-hit states may be without power for some time.
stories.background: Late-November storms often collide with the busiest travel days of the year. This one hit the Eastern Seaboard from Virginia to New York with wind, rain and king tides, while the West Coast also saw rough weather. The Macy's parade, a New York tradition since 1924, depends on giant helium balloons that cannot fly safely in strong winds. Utilities across several states were working to restore service as the storm moved off on Friday.

facts.text: Heavy winds and rain left more than 730,000 customers without power on Thursday evening, and roughly 2,100 flights had been delayed, according to the Wall Street Journal.
By Friday morning hundreds of thousands were still without power, with Pennsylvania and neighboring states hit hardest.
The storm brought torrential rain, high winds and flooding to parts of the East Coast from Virginia to New York.
King tides and large waves battered both the East and West coasts over the holiday period.
Macy's said Wednesday it was postponing the Thanksgiving Day Parade because of the weather, the first time in its history the parade has been postponed.
The parade was moved to Saturday; a Hawaii all-star band and hula group said the delay would cost them about $700,000.
The parade has been canceled outright only three times, Fox News reported.

stories.headline: EPA says no airborne lead detected after Army blows up explosive stockpile in Iowa
stories.summary: The Army detonated the nation's entire stockpile of lead azide, a chemical used to make explosives, at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant near Middletown on Wednesday. The EPA said its air monitors detected no airborne lead the next day, and lab results from samples at more than 130 nearby buildings could come as soon as Friday. Some residents remain worried, and the New York Times reported evidence that the Army knew of the risk much earlier.
stories.why_it_matters: Lead exposure is especially harmful to children, so the pending test results determine whether families near the plant need cleanup of homes, schools and farms.
stories.background: Lead azide is a highly sensitive compound used in detonators. The Army said its stored supply at the Iowa plant had degraded and become unstable, creating a risk of an uncontrolled explosion, so the EPA issued an emergency permit for a controlled blast that requires the Army to sample before and after, clean up contamination and report results. Before the blast, independent experts questioned the Army's modeling of how far lead dust could travel. The EPA is led by Administrator Lee Zeldin.

facts.text: The Army blew up the country's entire stockpile of lead azide in a controlled detonation in Iowa on Wednesday and said first checks showed it did not spread toxic dust to nearby homes and farms.
The detonation involved about five tons of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown.
EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said Thursday the agency's air monitors detected no airborne lead, while the agency awaits laboratory results from environmental samples.
The EPA said it sampled more than 130 structures, including homes, schools, daycare centers and churches, and that results could arrive Friday.
The White House called the detonation a success and said there was no health impact.
The New York Times reported that efforts to dispose of the unstable explosives began more than a year ago but were not completed.
The EPA's emergency permit requires the Army to notify nearby communities, sample before and after the blast, clean up contaminated areas and report findings.
Before the blast, The Intercept reported that experts found the Army's dispersion modeling incomplete and that it showed lead particles could reach as far as Maquoketa.

Focuses on what the Army knew and when, framing the blast as avoidable.

stories.headline: Trump calls pre-election GDP figures 'fake' and demands Commerce Department probe
stories.summary: In a Thanksgiving social media post, President Trump said economic growth figures released before this month's midterm elections were wrong and demanded an investigation of his own Commerce Department. His complaint followed an upward revision of third-quarter growth to a 4.3% annual rate. News outlets noted that he offered no evidence and that GDP revisions are routine.
stories.why_it_matters: Government statistics guide interest rates, wages and retirement plans; a president questioning his own agency's numbers raises concerns about whether the public will trust that data.
stories.background: Gross domestic product measures the total output of the economy, and the Commerce Department's Bureau of Economic Analysis publishes early estimates that it later revises as fuller data arrives. Republicans suffered heavy losses in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, which Democrats won broadly. Trump has previously attacked government statistics he disliked, including firing the head of the Bureau of Labor Statistics in 2025 after a weak jobs report.

The complaint came after third-quarter GDP growth was revised up to 4.3%.

stories.headline: Judge blocks FCC's early review of ABC station licenses on free-speech grounds
stories.summary: A federal judge on Wednesday blocked the Federal Communications Commission from moving ahead with an unusually early review of broadcast licenses held by Disney-owned ABC stations. Judge Loren AliKhan agreed with the network that the review was chilling its free-speech rights. ABC had sued in August, calling the review a Trump administration attack on speech it did not like.
stories.why_it_matters: The ruling limits, for now, how far federal regulators can use licensing power over TV stations in response to their programming, which affects what news and comedy viewers see.
stories.background: Local TV stations need FCC licenses that are normally renewed on a fixed schedule. Under Chairman Brendan Carr, the FCC ordered ABC's owned stations to seek renewal years early, which Disney argued was retaliation for content the president disliked. The FCC said it was looking at other issues, including Disney's employment practices, and argued the case belonged in an appeals court. The judge heard arguments in October before ruling this week.

stories.headline: China and other trading partners push back on Trump's new tariff plans
stories.summary: The Trump administration proposed new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China and the European Union. China said it reserves the right to take 'necessary measures', Brazil said it would not yield, and Japan also protested. The plan signals renewed pressure on China and on Asian economies that trade with both powers.
stories.why_it_matters: New tariffs are usually passed on at least partly to shoppers and businesses, so they could raise prices on imported goods and invite retaliation against U.S. exporters.
stories.background: Tariffs are taxes on imported goods, paid by the importing company. Trump has used them throughout his second term to pressure trading partners, sometimes announcing rates and later delaying or negotiating them down. This latest round targets many of America's biggest partners at once. Beijing, Brussels and Brasília have all clashed with Washington over trade before.

stories.headline: Musk and SpaceX pledge two SpaceX shares for every child's Trump Account
stories.summary: SpaceX said it would donate one share of its Class A stock to every active Trump Account, the government-backed savings accounts for children, and CEO Elon Musk said he would personally match it. SpaceX is now publicly traded, and Musk controls the company.

stories.headline: Drone attack in Kuwait kills two Italian technicians; Iran denies role
stories.summary: Two Italian technicians working for defense company Rheinmetall were killed Thursday when drones hit Kuwaiti military sites, including an air-defense station where they were working. Italy and Kuwait blamed Iran. Iran's foreign minister denied any involvement and called the incident suspicious.
stories.why_it_matters: Nobody had been killed in a strike on Kuwait for months. Deaths of European civilians at a Gulf base raise the risk that the US-Iran war spreads, and that keeps pressure on oil prices and Gulf shipping.
stories.background: The United States and Iran are at war, and talks to end it have stalled. In recent weeks, Gulf Arab states that host US military facilities, Kuwait among them, have come under repeated strikes. Italy has troops and contractors in Kuwait, and a drone hit an air base there hosting Italian and US forces in March without hurting anyone. Rheinmetall, a German arms maker, has an Italian unit that works on air-defense systems.

facts.text: Two Italian nationals were killed in a drone attack on a Kuwaiti military site on Thursday.
Italy's foreign ministry said the two were technicians for Rheinmetall, working on an air-defense system.
Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani said several Iranian-made drones targeted Kuwaiti military installations around 2 p.m., including an air-defense detection station.
Italy and Kuwait both confirmed the deaths and blamed Iran. It was the first fatal strike in Kuwait in months.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi denied Iran was responsible and called the incident "suspicious" and "a precooked recipe for war."
The attack follows weeks of strikes on Gulf Arab states that host US military facilities, with talks to end the war stalled.
President Trump said the war with Iran will end "whenever I want it" and that he is giving Iran "a chance to be smart."

stories.headline: New Zealand's ruling coalition falls one seat short; centrist newcomer holds the balance
stories.summary: Final results released Friday show Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's centre-right coalition one seat short of a majority. Luxon now needs the support of the centrist Opportunity Party, a newcomer led by Qiulae Wong, to stay in power. Without a deal, New Zealand could face another election.
stories.why_it_matters: A small new party now decides who governs New Zealand, so the next government's budget and policies will depend on what Opportunity asks for in return.
stories.background: New Zealand voted in early November, and the election-night count gave neither the right nor the left a clear win. Luxon leads the National Party, which has governed with two smaller right-leaning partners since 2023. Special votes, mostly from overseas and late voters, were still to be counted, and they decided the final seat allocation released on Friday. The Opportunity Party had never won seats in parliament before this election.

facts.text: Final general election results released Friday show the ruling centre-right coalition fell short of a parliamentary majority.

stories.headline: Trump says he asked Putin to pull back from Europe; Zelensky likens 'friend' remark to Hitler era
stories.summary: President Trump said Thursday that when he met Vladimir Putin in China last week, he asked him to pull back all military aggression against territories across Europe, and he hoped it would help produce a deal to end the war in Ukraine. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told the BBC that Trump calling Putin a 'friend' was strange, likened it to someone saying the same about Hitler during World War II, and said the US is not pushing Russia hard enough.
stories.why_it_matters: What Washington says to Moscow shapes the chances of a Ukraine peace deal and the security of European countries near Russia. That affects defense spending, energy prices and the risk of a wider war.
stories.background: Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, and the war continues. Trump has pushed for a negotiated settlement and has spoken warmly of Putin, calling him a friend as recently as last week. Trump and Putin met in China last week, on the sidelines of a summit. Zelensky has repeatedly urged the US to put more pressure on Moscow.

facts.text: Trump said Thursday he had asked Putin to "pull back all military aggression" against territories throughout Europe.
Trump said he made the request when the two met in China last week and that he thought it would help lead to a deal to end the war in Ukraine.

In a BBC interview, Zelensky called the Trump-Putin friendship "strange" and said Putin should not be treated as a friend.
Zelensky said Trump calling Putin a "friend" was the same as someone saying it about Hitler during World War II, while adding that what Trump says is up to him.
Zelensky said the US is not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks and urged Washington to increase pressure on Moscow.

stories.headline: Guinea-Bissau's military rulers push elections back to 2028
stories.summary: Guinea-Bissau's military government has postponed presidential and legislative elections until November 2028. In October, the transitional government said elections planned for December 2026 would have to be delayed, but it gave no new date then.

stories.headline: Stocks set to rally in a shortened Black Friday session as the AI trade rebounds
stories.summary: Global stocks rose after Thanksgiving as technology shares recovered from a bruising month of worries about artificial intelligence, and U.S. futures pointed to gains for Friday's half-day session. Investors moved out of safe havens: Treasuries slipped and yields rose, while copper and precious metals rallied. Next week's November jobs report and the Fed's Dec. 8-9 meeting are the next big tests.
stories.why_it_matters: A month of AI-driven swings has hit 401(k)s and index funds hard, and rising Treasury yields keep mortgage and loan rates high. A December Fed rate increase, which markets have been expecting, would push borrowing costs higher still.
stories.background: Shares of artificial-intelligence companies, led by chipmaker Nvidia, have fallen through November as investors question whether huge AI spending will pay off, and because a few of those companies make up a large share of the main indexes, the broader market has fallen with them. Turmoil at Nvidia, whose chief executive Jensen Huang resigned in mid-November and was then reinstated, has added to the swings. Inflation has also been rising, and a strong October jobs report led traders to expect the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates in December rather than cut them. U.S. markets were closed Thursday for Thanksgiving and close early on Friday.

stories.headline: Marlboro maker Altria weighs a possible bid for Britain's Imperial Brands
stories.summary: Imperial Brands, the British tobacco company, confirmed that Altria is considering a possible offer for it, and Imperial's shares jumped in London. stories.why_it_matters: A deal would reshape one of the world's largest consumer industries as smoking declines; for most people the effect is through retirement funds and index funds that hold tobacco shares. Coverage came mainly from business and center-rated outlets.
stories.background: Altria sells Marlboro cigarettes in the United States, and Imperial Brands is a British company that makes brands such as Winston and Davidoff. stories.headline: Thanksgiving storm floods coastal NYC and pushes Macy's parade to Saturday
stories.summary: A wind and rain storm hit New York City on Thanksgiving Day, flooding coastal areas, snarling holiday travel and leading organizers to postpone the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade for the first time. CBS News and CNN reported the parade was rescheduled for Saturday, Nov. 28. Gov. Kathy Hochul had declared a state of emergency for southern New York ahead of the storm.
stories.why_it_matters: New Yorkers who planned to attend or work the parade need to plan for Saturday instead, and residents of low-lying neighborhoods faced flooding and outages during one of the year's busiest travel days.
stories.background: The Macy's parade has run along Manhattan's West Side on Thanksgiving morning for about a century, and its giant balloons are vulnerable to strong gusts funneled between skyscrapers; balloons have been grounded in the past, but the whole parade had never been moved. This year a large storm system brought heavy rain, high winds and high tides to much of the country, including the East Coast. State officials declared an emergency the day before, and city emergency managers issued travel guidance. Mayor Zohran Mamdani's administration handled the city response.

facts.text: The Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade was postponed for the first time in its history.
CBS News and CNN reported the parade was rescheduled for Saturday, Nov. 28, with Macy's citing the risk of wind damaging the balloons.
Nearly a million customers lost power along the East Coast, according to the AP report carried by The Guardian.
More than 2,000 flights were delayed or canceled as the storm moved up the East Coast.
High tides flooded coastal areas including parts of Staten Island, and the city's emergency management office reported 1.5 to 2 inches of rain, according to CBS News.
Mayor Mamdani said two people were rescued from cars caught in flooding, CBS News reported.
Gov. Kathy Hochul declared a state of emergency for southern New York on Nov. 25.
Gothamist reported the worst of the storm was expected from 4 p.m. to 10 p.m. Thursday, as city and state officials urged caution for holiday travel.

stories.headline: Post reports NYPD's disbanded protest unit was deployed to a Brooklyn protest
stories.summary: The New York Post reported that NYPD Strategic Response Group officers were sent to handle an anti-Israel protest in Brooklyn, about 10 days after Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced the unit was being disbanded. The Post quoted an unnamed Brooklyn officer saying the unit was the only way to deal with violent protests. The city's account of the deployment was not available in the material reviewed.
stories.why_it_matters: How the city polices protests while it dismantles the SRG affects demonstrators' rights and public safety; only a right-leaning outlet covered this deployment in the material ingested today.
stories.background: The Strategic Response Group was created in 2015 to handle both counterterrorism deployments and large protests, and civil liberties groups criticized its tactics during the 2020 protests. Mayor Mamdani campaigned on disbanding it and announced on Nov. 16, with Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch, that counterterrorism duties would move to the Intelligence and Counterterrorism Bureau and protest response to a new civilian-led structure, with kettling banned. Tisch said the NYPD's response to large crowds or civil disorder would not change. Police unions and some Council members opposed the move.

stories.summary: A 42-year-old man was beaten into critical condition on a Manhattan-bound D train in Brooklyn on Wednesday night after he asked a group of teenagers to be quiet, according to police and sources cited by the New York Post. stories.headline: Large Democratic freshman class could decide long-stalled bills in Albany
stories.summary: Gothamist reported that 27 new Democrats will join the state Legislature in January, with Democrats controlling at least 158 of its 213 seats. The Assembly in particular is preparing for a large freshman class, which could affect the fate of bills that have stalled in past sessions.
stories.why_it_matters: Who sits in Albany shapes rent rules, transit funding and school policy for the city, so a large turnover can change which long-debated bills reach a vote.
stories.background: New York's Legislature has an Assembly of 150 members and a Senate of 63, both controlled by Democrats. Many bills pass one chamber and stall in the other, often because leaders such as Assembly Speaker Carl Heastie do not bring them to the floor. The November elections produced a wave of new members, many from the city. The new session begins in January alongside budget talks with Gov. Kathy Hochul.

stories.headline: City lifts vacate orders on two buildings beside deadly Flatbush collapse
stories.summary: The Daily News reported that vacate orders were lifted on two properties next to the Brooklyn building that collapsed this month and killed eight people. The collapsed building at 1321 Flatbush Avenue remains slated for demolition, and a criminal investigation into work at a neighboring site continues.
stories.why_it_matters: Some displaced neighbors may be able to return home, while the city's handling of the collapse bears on building safety rules across the five boroughs.
stories.background: A three-story building at 1321 Flatbush Avenue collapsed on Nov. 11, killing eight people and injuring at least 18. City records showed contractors at a neighboring construction site had violated a stop-work order, and a criminal investigation followed. Engineers found the remaining structure too dangerous to save, and nearby buildings were ordered vacated. The city has been housing displaced residents in hotels through the end of November, and Mayor Mamdani ordered a broader review of construction sites.

concept.explanation: Key-person risk is the danger that a company's value depends heavily on one individual, usually a founder or chief executive, so that their departure, illness or scandal can knock down the stock. Investors price it in when a leader is seen as hard to replace, and it moves sharply on news about that person, as Nvidia's swings around Jensen Huang's exit and return showed. It reaches your wallet because giant companies like Nvidia make up a large share of index funds held in 401(k)s and IRAs, so one person's fortunes can move many people's retirement balances.
